# Alcohol use disorder

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Emergency medicine > Psychiatric disorders > Alcohol use disorder*

[Original Article Link](/library/h80cm3)

---

## Summary

<u>Alcohol</u> use disorder (AUD) is a chronic condition in which a pattern of <u>alcohol</u> use leads to significant physical and psychosocial impairment or <u>distress</u>. Not all individuals with <u>heavy alcohol use</u> develop AUD, and not all individuals with AUD have a history of <u>heavy alcohol use</u>. If <u>screening for unhealthy alcohol use</u> suggests AUD, diagnosis is confirmed using the <u>DSM-5 criteria for AUD</u>. An <u>evaluation for alcohol-related complications</u> is recommended at the point of diagnosis for early identification and treatment. The <u>management of AUD</u> depends on whether the patient wishes to reduce their <u>alcohol</u> consumption. For patients who want to reduce their intake or abstain from <u>alcohol</u>, <u>psychotherapy</u> and/or <u>pharmacotherapy for AUD</u> may be utilized. For patients who do not wish or are unable to change their <u>alcohol</u> use, the mainstays of management are <u>harm reduction strategies</u> and regular monitoring for <u>complications of alcohol use</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>Prevalence</u> [[2]](/library/cJaaGl)

* Lifetime <u>prevalence</u> is ∼ 29%.

* More common in White and Native American individuals

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 18–25 years [[3]](/library/7GW40M0)

* Sex: <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u> (2.5:1) [[4]](/library/Nta-dm)

* Associated comorbidities [[2]](/library/cJaaGl)

* <u>Personality disorders</u> (most commonly <u>borderline personality disorder</u>)

* <u>Anxiety</u>, <u>mood disorders</u> (e.g., <u>depression</u>, <u>bipolar disorder</u>), <u>posttraumatic stress disorder</u>, and <u>psychosis</u>

* Other substance-related disorders (e.g., stimulants, sedatives, <u>cannabis</u>)

* <u>Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder</u>




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Diagnosis

### General principles




* AUD is normally detected during <u>screening for unhealthy alcohol use</u>.

* The diagnosis is confirmed if <u>DSM-5 criteria for AUD</u> are met.

* For patients who meet the <u>DSM-5 criteria for AUD</u>, perform diagnostic studies for:

* <u>Laboratory confirmation of alcohol use</u>

* <u>Evaluation for alcohol-related complications</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Liver chemistries</u> and an abdominal <u>ultrasound</u> are recommended for all patients with AUD to assess for <u>alcohol-associated liver disease</u>. [[8]](/library/Rlbl9F)




### <u>DSM-5</u> diagnostic criteria [[9]](/library/MEcMwV0)[[10]](/library/QjWuZl0)




| DSM-5 criteria for alcohol use disorder |  |
| --- | --- |
| Definition | <br>* A pattern of <u>alcohol</u> use that causes significant physical and psychosocial impairment or <u>distress</u><br><br> |
| Criteria | <br><br>* Strong urge to drink <u>alcohol</u><br><br>* Drinking more or over a longer period than intended<br><br>* An increasing amount of <u>alcohol</u> is needed to achieve the same effects.<br><br>* Unsuccessful attempts to reduce or stop <u>alcohol</u> intake<br><br>* Lots of time is spent obtaining <u>alcohol</u>, drinking, or recovering from its effects.<br><br>* Cessation of drinking causes <u>clinical features of alcohol withdrawal</u>.<br><br>* Drinking results in an inability to fulfill daily tasks (e.g., at work, home, or school).<br><br>* Continued drinking despite consequent social or interpersonal problems<br><br>* Drinking has resulted in giving up important interests and activities.<br><br>* <u>Alcohol</u> use leads to situations that can cause physical harm (e.g., unsafe driving).<br><br>* Continued drinking despite knowledge that physical or psychological problems are likely due to <u>alcohol</u> use<br><br><br> |
| <br><br>* AUD is diagnosed if ≥ 2 criteria are present within the past 12 months.<br><br>* Severity<br><br>* Mild: 2–3 criteria<br><br>* Moderate: 4–5 criteria<br><br>* Severe: ≥ 6 criteria<br><br><br> |  |

## Initial management

### All patients [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)




* Urgently treat acute complications of AUD; see: [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[12]](/library/dIWob50)

* “<u>Management of alcohol withdrawal</u>”

* “<u>Management of Wernicke encephalopathy</u>”

* “<u>Management of alcohol intoxication</u>”

* Provide <u>counseling on AUD</u>.

* Educate patients on the health <u>complications of alcohol use</u>.

* Discuss the risk of harm to others; follow state law for mandatory reporting requirements.

* Screen for and treat comorbid psychiatric conditions (e.g., <u>depression</u>). [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)

* Assess the patient's insight and motivation to make changes.   [[13]](/library/KIWUd50)

* Discuss lifestyle modifications to reduce the risk of <u>complications of alcohol use</u>.

* Encourage healthy eating. [[14]](/library/6GWjZM0)

* Refer to food banks and other <u>nutritional support</u> programs if needed.

* Consider multivitamins containing <u>vitamin B<sub>1</sub></u> (<u>thiamine</u>), <u>vitamin B<sub>6</sub></u> (<u>pyridoxine</u>), and <u>folic acid</u>.  [[14]](/library/6GWjZM0)[[15]](/library/OMWIKN0)

* Discuss <u>smoking cessation</u>.  [[16]](/library/JGWsZM0)[[17]](/library/pGWLZM0)

* Encourage the patient to involve individuals (e.g., family, friends) who can provide support. [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[12]](/library/dIWob50)[[18]](/library/VIWGb50)





> [!TIP]
> Friends and family of patients with AUD can experience significant <u>distress</u>; offer support, including referral to community support groups for family and friends such as Al-Anon. [[19]](/library/wGWhYM0)




![Transtheoretical model of behavioral change](media/wy7zthn1q9od184s725oqgsl.jpg)

Transtheoretical model of behavioral change




### Patients who want <u>treatment for AUD</u>




* Create and document a plan based on the patient's goals, using <u>shared decision-making</u>.  [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)

* Refer for <u>psychotherapy</u>, e.g., <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u> and <u>family therapy</u>.  [[18]](/library/VIWGb50)[[20]](/library/-nXDDA)

* Provide resources for community support groups, e.g., <u>Alcoholics Anonymous</u>. [[13]](/library/KIWUd50)[[21]](/library/THW6p50)

* Patients with moderate to severe AUD: Offer <u>medication-assisted treatment</u> (see “<u>Pharmacotherapy for AUD</u>”).

* Identify potential triggers that can cause relapse. [[13]](/library/KIWUd50)[[18]](/library/VIWGb50)

* Schedule follow-up visits to monitor for clinical improvement and <u>treatment adherence</u>; adjust management as necessary. [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[12]](/library/dIWob50)





> [!TIP]
> For patients with a court-mandated treatment plan, ascertain the testing and reporting requirements. [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)




### Patients who do not want <u>treatment for AUD</u>




* Use <u>patient-centered care</u>.

* Discuss harm mitigation strategies.

* Advise patients they can return at any point to start treatment.

* Regularly review patients for <u>complications of alcohol use</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Psychosocial therapy can improve <u>treatment adherence</u> and outcomes and should be offered to all patients. [[12]](/library/dIWob50)

---

## Initiation of pharmacotherapy

### Indications [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[18]](/library/VIWGb50)[[21]](/library/THW6p50)




* Individuals ; with moderate to severe AUD who want to decrease the amount of <u>alcohol</u> consumed or abstain from use  [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[18]](/library/VIWGb50)[[22]](/library/CDcqge0)

* Consider on a case-by-case basis for patients with mild AUD who have either: [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)

* A preference for pharmacotherapy

* An insufficient response to nonpharmacological treatments





### Choice of medication




#### Approach




* Obtain baseline <u>laboratory studies</u> to ascertain suitable medications.

* <u>CBC</u>

* <u>Liver chemistries</u>  [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)

* Renal function  [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[18]](/library/VIWGb50)

* Urine toxicology  [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)

* <u>Pregnancy test</u>  [[23]](/library/ktWmdM0)

* Determine whether the patient is abstaining, or plans to abstain, from <u>alcohol</u> use.  [[21]](/library/THW6p50)

* Screen for comorbidities, e.g., <u>opioid use disorder</u> (<u>OUD</u>).  [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)

* Inquire about <u>risk factors for poor adherence</u>.

* Check if patients receiving court-mandated treatment require a particular pharmacotherapy. [[24]](/library/OtWIdM0)





> [!TIP]
> Give patients a wallet card with details of their <u>medication-assisted treatment</u> to show medical personnel in the event of an emergency or if a procedure is needed (e.g., dental <u>surgery</u>). [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[12]](/library/dIWob50)




#### First-line options [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[21]](/library/THW6p50)




* <u>Naltrexone</u> and <u>acamprosate</u> are preferred.  [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[21]](/library/THW6p50)

* Both medications reduce cravings and can be used for patients who: [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[18]](/library/VIWGb50)

* Continue to drink <u>alcohol</u>

* Use other substances recreationally

* Interactions with other medications are minimal. [[18]](/library/VIWGb50)





##### <u>Naltrexone</u>




* <u>Naltrexone</u> DOSAGE can be given orally or IM.  [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[12]](/library/dIWob50)[[18]](/library/VIWGb50)

* Mechanism of action: central <u>μ-opioid receptor</u> <u>antagonist</u>

* Considerations

* Check <u>liver chemistries</u> before and after starting <u>naltrexone</u> because of the risk of hepatic dysfunction in patients with <u>liver</u> disease.  [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)

* Advise patients to abstain from <u>opioid</u> use 7–14 days before starting <u>naltrexone</u>.  [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)





##### Acamprosate [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[18]](/library/VIWGb50)




* <u>Acamprosate</u> DOSAGE requires frequent oral dosing to be effective.  [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[18]](/library/VIWGb50)

* Mechanism of action: may modulate central <u>glutamate</u> <u>receptors</u> [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[18]](/library/VIWGb50)

* Considerations: Check serum <u>creatinine</u> before initiating treatment.  [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[18]](/library/VIWGb50)





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid concurrent use of <u>opioids</u> and <u>naltrexone</u> because of the risk of <u>opioid withdrawal</u>. [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)




#### Alternative options




Alternative medications may be considered, especially for patients who do not improve with first-line options. [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)




##### Disulfiram




* <u>Disulfiram</u> DOSAGE is given orally once daily. [[18]](/library/VIWGb50)

* Deters patients from drinking <u>alcohol</u> by precipitating a disulfiram-alcohol reaction; symptoms include ; :  [[25]](/library/itWJWM0)[[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[27]](/library/QtWuWM0)

* Cutaneous <u>vasodilation</u>

* <u>Headache</u>

* <u>Nausea and vomiting</u>

* <u>Tachycardia</u> and other <u>cardiac arrhythmias</u>

* <u>Hypotension</u>

* <u>Seizures</u>

* Breathing difficulties (including <u>bronchospasm</u> and <u>dyspnea</u>)

* To prevent <u>disulfiram</u>-<u>alcohol</u> reactions: [[18]](/library/VIWGb50)
* Ensure patients have been abstinent for at least 12 hours before starting <u>disulfiram</u>.  [[21]](/library/THW6p50)
* Advise patients to maintain abstinence during treatment and for 14 days after.  [[18]](/library/VIWGb50)

* Considerations

* Check <u>liver</u> <u>transaminases</u> before and up to 2 weeks after starting treatment; although rare, a rise in enzyme levels can occur. [[12]](/library/dIWob50)

* Consider obtaining a <u>baseline ECG</u> for at-risk individuals (e.g., those with a history of cardiac disease).  [[12]](/library/dIWob50)

* Do not prescribe if patients have recently received <u>metronidazole</u>, because of the risk of <u>psychosis</u>. [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)

* Not recommended for initiation in the emergency department because monitoring is required. [[15]](/library/OMWIKN0)





> [!WARNING]
> During treatment with <u>disulfiram</u>, advise <u>alcohol</u> abstinence, avoidance of <u>alcohol</u>-containing products (e.g., some mouthwashes), and certain medications such as <u>metronidazole</u>. [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[15]](/library/OMWIKN0)[[18]](/library/VIWGb50)




![Ethanol metabolism](media/kym1b7i25x0ix7vq0zmh4zzm.jpg)

Ethanol metabolism




##### <u>Topiramate</u>




* <u>Topiramate</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE is given orally and requires slow <u>titration</u>. [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[21]](/library/THW6p50)

* Reduces cravings (and can assist in weight loss)





##### <u>Gabapentin</u>




* <u>Gabapentin</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE is given orally and requires slow <u>titration</u>. [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)

* Reduces cravings and may help with comorbid <u>anxiety</u>  [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[28]](/library/4tW3dM0)

* Has the potential for misuse; monitor patients carefully. [[11]](/library/eIWxb50)[[29]](/library/jtW_WM0)

## Complications

See also “<u>Complications of alcohol use</u>.”




### Alcoholic ketoacidosis [[26]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Definition: elevated <u>anion gap metabolic acidosis</u> due to increased production of <u>ketone bodies</u> with normal or low <u>glucose</u> levels resulting from the combined effects of <u>alcohol</u> and <u>starvation</u> on <u>glucose metabolism</u>

* Etiology

* Most commonly occurs in <u>malnourished</u> individuals with AUD

* Associated with recent episodes of <u>binge drinking</u> complicated by poor food intake, <u>dehydration</u>, and <u>vomiting</u>

* Onset: typically occurs 1–3 days after <u>binge drinking</u>

* Pathophysiology: accumulation of <u>ketone bodies</u> (see <u>ketogenesis</u>) as a result of:

* Depleted <u>glycogen</u> stores in the <u>liver</u> (<u>malnutrition</u>/decreased <u>carbohydrate</u> intake)

* Increased <u>lipolysis</u> and free <u>fatty acid</u> release

* Decreased energy intake (e.g., <u>starvation</u>) → decreased <u>insulin</u> secretion and excess secretion of <u>glucagon</u>, <u>catecholamines</u>, and <u>cortisol</u>

* Increased <u>NADH</u>:<u>NAD<sup>+</sup></u> <u>ratio</u>: regular <u>heavy alcohol use</u> ;   → impaired hepatic <u>gluconeogenesis</u> → <u>hypoglycemia</u> → decreased <u>insulin</u> secretion

* <u>Volume depletion</u> (e.g., <u>vomiting</u>, poor oral fluid intake) → impaired renal <u>perfusion</u> → decreased ability to excrete <u>ketone bodies</u>

* Clinical features of alcoholic ketosis

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, and abdominal <u>pain</u>

* <u>Tachypnea</u>

* Features of <u>dehydration</u> and <u>electrolyte</u> imbalance (e.g., <u>hyponatremia</u>, <u>hypokalemia</u>, <u>hypophosphatemia</u>), including <u>hypotension</u> and <u>altered mental status</u>

* Features of <u>alcohol withdrawal</u>: e.g., <u>tremors</u>, <u>seizures</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>

* Diagnostics

* <u>Arterial blood gas analysis</u>: <u>elevated anion gap metabolic acidosis</u>

* <u>Ketonemia</u> (<u>acetoacetate</u>, <u>β-hydroxybutyrate</u>, acetone in blood) and <u>ketonuria</u>

* Blood <u>glucose</u>: low, normal, or only moderately increased

* Blood ethanol: not detectable or low [[31]](/library/4HY3qq)

* Treatment

* Initially: parenteral administration of <u>thiamine</u> to prevent <u>Wernicke encephalopathy</u>

* Followed by: <u>IV fluid therapy</u> with 5% dextrose in 0.9% saline

* <u>Correction of electrolyte imbalances</u>

* <u>Treatment of alcohol withdrawal</u> and <u>complications of alcohol use</u>

* Prognosis: The condition is reversible with appropriate treatment.





> [!TIP]
> In contrast to <u>diabetic ketoacidosis</u>, blood <u>glucose</u> levels are normal or low in <u>alcoholic ketoacidosis</u>.
